chapter.title: Chord Fundamentals and Chord Exercises (Lessons 1-5)
chapter.summary: Establishes the 26-chord numbered catalog, declares rhythm strumming obsolete, installs the chromatic up-the-neck drill, mandates transposition as the definition of mastery, restricts the rhythm palette to Chords 1-6 in four foundational keys, and introduces the two-line standard-vs-new substitution format.

sections.title: Replacing strummed chords
sections.summary: Baker declares the old strumming style obsolete and announces the replacement system powering chord solos, intros, backgrounds, and fill-ins.

engine_rules.name: Reject static strumming in favor of voicing motion
engine_rules.falsifier: A plain two-bar strum appears in a Baker arrangement without substitution
engine_rules.anchor: The old style of strumming chords for guitar will never do in modern playing, so we will have to work out a complete system.

paragraphs.summary: States the book's central premise: rhythm strumming is obsolete and must be replaced by a systematic vocabulary.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: The old style of strumming chords for guitar will never do in modern playing, so we will have to work out a complete system.

sections.title: The 26 essential chords
sections.summary: Prunes the guitar's chord universe to 26 essential, numbered shapes and dismisses the remainder as meaningless.

engine_rules.name: Draw voicings exclusively from the 26-to-30 numbered catalog
engine_rules.falsifier: A voicing outside the numbered 1-30 catalog is prescribed as a primary chord choice
engine_rules.anchor: Below you have 26 chords which you must learn to use right away. There are more chords to learn, but these are the most important.

paragraphs.summary: Defines the curated 26-chord vocabulary and rationalizes the radical pruning.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Below you have 26 chords which you must learn to use right away.

sections.title: Two starting keys
sections.summary: Anchors the method in G and C as seed keys from which every other key is derived by transposition.

engine_rules.name: Ground initial chord exercises in G major and C major as seed keys
engine_rules.falsifier: Exercises are introduced in a key other than G or C before those keys are mastered
engine_rules.anchor: If you will notice, some of these chords are designed for the key of G major and some for C major. These are the two keys that we are going to work with first.

paragraphs.summary: Establishes G and C as the two primary training keys.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: If you will notice, some of these chords are designed for the key of G major and some for C major.

sections.title: Transposition is mandatory
sections.summary: Elevates transposition from study aid to the single non-negotiable practice defining mastery.

engine_rules.name: Transpose every learned voicing to all remaining keys
engine_rules.falsifier: A Baker prescription is practiced in only one key and the lesson advances without transposition
engine_rules.anchor: It is very important that everything in the book be transposed to all of the other keys. You should be able to play any song in any key by the time you finish this book, and learning to transpose is the only thing that can help you to do this.

paragraphs.summary: States the transposition mandate as the single path to full mastery.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: It is very important that everything in the book be transposed to all of the other keys.

sections.title: Chromatic chord exercise
sections.summary: Baker's signature drill: move each chord shape chromatically up the neck to internalize voicings as portable hand-shapes.

engine_rules.name: Internalize every new shape by sliding it chromatically up and down the neck
engine_rules.falsifier: A new chord shape is learned only in one fret position without chromatic movement
engine_rules.anchor: Take your G Chords which are the first three chords in Lesson One, and practice them chromatically always up the neck of your guitar as shown below.

paragraphs.summary: Establishes chromatic movement as the internalization mechanism for all chord shapes.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Take your G Chords which are the first three chords in Lesson One, and practice them chromatically always up the neck of your guitar as shown below.

sections.title: Six core rhythm chords
sections.summary: Restricts the rhythm-chord palette to the numbered Chords 1-6 for all comping exercises.

engine_rules.name: Restrict comping palette to Chords No. 1-6 for rhythm exercises
engine_rules.falsifier: Chords 7 or higher are prescribed as primary rhythm voicings in the foundational key exercises
engine_rules.anchor: By the way, you are only using Chords No. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 for these Exercises. Just transpose them to the proper keys.

paragraphs.summary: Restricts the rhythm-chord palette to a tight numbered set.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: By the way, you are only using Chords No. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 for these Exercises.

sections.title: Standard vs. new chords
sections.summary: Introduces the two-line standard/new substitution format that becomes the dominant pedagogical device of the book.

engine_rules.name: Display every substitution in the two-line standard-above / new-below format
engine_rules.falsifier: A Baker substitution is presented without both the original and the new change visible together
engine_rules.anchor: First, I'm going to write out the standard changes as they are in some songs, and below them I will write the new ones, the way they should be played against the old ones.

paragraphs.summary: Introduces the standard-vs-new two-line pedagogical format.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: First, I'm going to write out the standard changes as they are in some songs, and below them I will write the new ones, the way they should be played against the old ones.

chapter.title: Melody Chord Progressions, Introductions, Arpeggio and String Bass Styles (Lessons 6-8)
chapter.summary: Pivots from rhythm comping to melody-chord playing and intros; elevates arpeggio and walking string-bass above strumming; establishes combinatorial intro-generation from a small fixed chord set by varying rhythm.

sections.title: Chromatic intro practice
sections.summary: Reapplies the chromatic-up-the-neck drill specifically to intro shapes.

engine_rules.name: Internalize intro shapes by practicing them chromatically up and down the fingerboard
engine_rules.falsifier: An intro shape is rehearsed only in its written key without chromatic movement
engine_rules.anchor: You may find some of these very hard to play, but if you practice them chromatically up and down the finger board you will soon become accustomed to them.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes chromatic fingerboard practice specifically for difficult intro shapes.
key_phrases: up and down the finger board
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: if you practice them chromatically up and down the finger board you will soon become accustomed to them.

sections.title: Vary rhythm to create intros
sections.summary: Introduces rhythmic-displacement (root-then-chord, arpeggiation) as Baker's method for generating unlimited intros from a fixed chord set.

engine_rules.name: Generate new intros by displacing rhythm: root-first then chord, or arpeggiated
engine_rules.falsifier: A new intro is generated by adding new chord shapes rather than by rhythmically reordering an existing fixed set
engine_rules.anchor: Another way to get new ideas is to change the rhythm of the introduction. Try playing them in arpeggio style, or try playing the bottom note of the chord first, then the chord.

paragraphs.summary: States the rhythmic-displacement trick as the go-to method for new intro generation.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Another way to get new ideas is to change the rhythm of the introduction. Try playing them in arpeggio style, or try playing the bottom note of the chord first, then the chord.

sections.title: Arpeggio and string bass styles
sections.summary: Names arpeggio and walking string-bass as the two characteristic accompaniment textures elevated above plain strumming.

engine_rules.name: Prefer arpeggio or walking string-bass texture over plain strumming in any accompaniment context
engine_rules.falsifier: Plain block strumming is prescribed as the primary texture for a comping or backing context
engine_rules.anchor: In this Lesson I have a few ideas on how to use the Arpeggio, and the string bass.

paragraphs.summary: Introduces arpeggio and string-bass as the two elevation textures.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: In this Lesson I have a few ideas on how to use the Arpeggio, and the string bass.

chapter.title: Chords in C/Db/Eb, Harmonic Structure and Chord Progressing (Lessons 9-12)
chapter.summary: Opens the C/Db/Eb key cluster, installs the major/minor/dominant substitution axioms, articulates the corny-vs-colorful aesthetic, and mandates twelve daily repetitions for chord-progressing exercises.

sections.title: Major triad substitution rule
sections.summary: States the substitution axiom that licenses replacing every plain major chord with Cma7/ma6/ma9 voicings.

engine_rules.name: Replace any plain major triad with a maj7, maj6, or maj9 voicing from the catalog
engine_rules.falsifier: A plain major triad is left unchanged without at least one extension voicing offered as substitution
engine_rules.anchor: Now then, any chord on a major mode can be used in place of the major triad.

paragraphs.summary: States the major-mode substitution axiom.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Now then, any chord on a major mode can be used in place of the major triad.

sections.title: Avoid strumming for color
sections.summary: Articulates Baker's aesthetic motivation: static strumming is 'corny', motion through adaptable voicings is jazz.

engine_rules.name: Add harmonic color to any two-bar static chord by inserting an adaptable voicing progression
engine_rules.falsifier: A two-bar static major chord appears in a Baker arrangement without any motion through adapted voicings
engine_rules.anchor: We don't want to strum a C major chord for the whole two bars, because it doesn't have enough color, and besides it sounds corny, so we add color by using progressions that are adaptable as follows

paragraphs.summary: Declares static strumming corny and prescribes adaptable progressions for color.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: We don't want to strum a C major chord for the whole two bars, because it doesn't have enough color, and besides it sounds corny, so we add color by using progressions that are adaptable as follows

sections.title: Minor and dominant substitution
sections.summary: Extends the substitution rule from major to minor and dominant chords and enumerates the full dominant-extension menu.

engine_rules.name: Replace any plain minor chord with a min6, min7, or min9 voicing
engine_rules.falsifier: A plain minor triad is left unchanged in a Baker arrangement
engine_rules.anchor: if you have a Dmi chord (Any minor chord can be used on the minor mode) Dmi6, Dmi7 and Dmi9 are adaptable, because they are all on the same mode.

engine_rules.name: Expand any dominant-7 chord with the full extension menu: 13, 9, 7#5+9, 13#5+9, 7b5, 11, 13b9
engine_rules.falsifier: A plain dom7 chord is left unaltered in any Baker comping or solo context without a substitution being offered
engine_rules.anchor: With dominant chords there is no limit to what can be done. For instance if you have a G7 Chord — you could use G13, G9, G7#5+9, G13#549, G75, G11, G1349 and so on.

paragraphs.summary: Enumerates the minor and dominant substitution menus.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: With dominant chords there is no limit to what can be done. For instance if you have a G7 Chord — you could use G13, G9, G7#5+9, G13#549, G75, G11, G1349 and so on.

sections.title: Substitutions need progression
sections.summary: Constrains the substitution licence: voicing choices are governed by voice-leading and progression context, not free swap.

engine_rules.name: Require substitution candidates to serve voice-leading in context; reject arbitrary insertion
engine_rules.falsifier: Baker prescribes inserting any extended voicing regardless of the preceding and following chord's voice-leading
engine_rules.anchor: It all depends on how the chords are progressing. You just can't throw these chords in any place, they have to be part of some kind of progression.

paragraphs.summary: States that substitutions must serve an actual progression.
key_phrases: part of some kind of progression
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: It all depends on how the chords are progressing. You just can't throw these chords in any place, they have to be part of some kind of progression.

chapter.title: Vamps and Fill-ins (Lessons 13-14)
chapter.summary: States the two-positions-per-key doctrine, codifies the dominant-to-relative-minor substitution as a twelve-row written chart, introduces vamps as a jump/novelty genre unit, specifies the seven-key transposition target for vamps, and reapplies arpeggio/string-bass textures to vamps.

sections.title: Two position sets per key
sections.summary: States that Baker's system uses only two position sets per key (in C: 3rd and 8th), eliminating unnecessary chord shapes.

engine_rules.name: Assign exactly two governing position sets to each key; in C major use 3rd and 8th positions
engine_rules.falsifier: More than two position sets are prescribed for a single key
engine_rules.anchor: With our new chords we only have two sets for each key. Like in the key of C major, one set of chords starts at the third position and the other set at the 8th position.

paragraphs.summary: States the two-positions-per-key doctrine as Baker's central voicing-architecture claim.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: With our new chords we only have two sets for each key. Like in the key of C major, one set of chords starts at the third position and the other set at the 8th position.

sections.title: Tritone-sub via relative minor
sections.summary: Defines Baker's ii-for-V substitution rule: replace any V7 with the minor a fifth above (the relative minor of the dominant).

engine_rules.name: Substitute any dominant-7 chord with the minor-7 built on its fifth (relative minor)
engine_rules.falsifier: The fifth-above minor substitution is not offered when a dominant chord occupies a two-bar holding zone
engine_rules.anchor: the 5th of any dominant chord can be substituted in place of the Dominant itself. Let's say that you have two bars of D7. All right, the 5th of D is A. A-minor is a very close relative to D7. Now you know that if you have a dominant 7 chord you can substitute its relative minor which is the 5th of the chord.

engine_rules.name: Build a twelve-row dominant/relative-minor chart from C7 through B7 before applying the substitution
engine_rules.falsifier: The substitution is applied without the student having constructed the twelve-row written chart
engine_rules.anchor: you must write out all dominant 7 chords from C7 up to B7 and beside them put the relative minor like this: — the 5th of C7 is G minor

paragraphs.summary: Codifies the relative-minor substitution and its chart-building drill.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: the 5th of any dominant chord can be substituted in place of the Dominant itself.

sections.title: Transpose vamps to seven keys
sections.summary: Specifies the seven-key transposition target list (Db, Eb, F, G, A, Bb plus home C) for the vamp study.
key_phrases: Db Eb F G A Bb

engine_rules.name: Transpose vamps to exactly seven keys: Db, Eb, F, G, A, Bb (plus home C), building charts for each
engine_rules.falsifier: Vamp transposition stops short of all seven target keys
engine_rules.anchor: After you have worked these vamps out in this key which is C major, transpose them to the keys of: Dé, Eé, F, G, A, and Bé, then make up charts similar to this one in each key.

paragraphs.summary: Specifies the exact seven-key transposition target for vamp study.
key_phrases: Db Eb F G A Bb
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: After you have worked these vamps out in this key which is C major, transpose them to the keys of: Dé, Eé, F, G, A, and Bé, then make up charts similar to this one in each key.

chapter.title: Bridges and Last Lesson in Chord Progressions (Lessons 15-16)
chapter.summary: Extends the chord catalog to 30 with open-string-root vamp voicings, acknowledges that some shapes can't be uniformly transposed, introduces bridges in the standard/new format, and elevates the dominant-as-leading-chord principle with its three-category taxonomy to capstone status (Lesson 16).

sections.title: New chords 27-30
sections.summary: Extends the numbered catalog to chords 27-30: open-string-root voicings for horn-backing fill-ins.

engine_rules.name: Add Chords 27-30 (open-string-root vamp voicings) for horn-backing fill-ins in G major
engine_rules.falsifier: Chords 27-30 are prescribed in a key whose open-string-root voicings are not available
engine_rules.anchor: In order to work out these vamps, I will have to introduce a few new chords. We will call them chords No. 27, 28, 29 and 30.

paragraphs.summary: Names Chords 27-30 as the new fill-in vamp voicings.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: In order to work out these vamps, I will have to introduce a few new chords. We will call them chords No. 27, 28, 29 and 30.

sections.title: Some shapes don't transpose
sections.summary: Acknowledges that open-string-root vamp shapes are key-specific and cannot be uniformly transposed.
key_phrases: can't play them all in every key

engine_rules.name: Treat open-string-root vamp shapes (Chords 27-30) as key-specific; select per key rather than uniformly shift
engine_rules.falsifier: Chords 27-30 are uniformly transposed chromatically rather than selected per key
engine_rules.anchor: you can't play them all in every key.

sections.title: Dominant as leading chord
sections.summary: Elevates Lesson 16 to capstone status: the dominant-as-leading-chord principle unifies every chord-connection scheme in the book.

engine_rules.name: Insert an appropriate dominant chord as the leading chord between any two non-dominant chords
engine_rules.falsifier: Two non-adjacent chords are connected without an intervening dominant leading chord in a Baker arrangement
engine_rules.anchor: This Lesson is the key to all of the other lessons. Here I have written out the best possible way to connect one chord to another using the dominant as leading chord for each example.

paragraphs.summary: Declares the dominant-as-leading-chord principle as the key to every other lesson.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: This Lesson is the key to all of the other lessons. Here I have written out the best possible way to connect one chord to another using the dominant as leading chord for each example.

sections.title: Three connection categories
sections.summary: Defines the three-category taxonomy (V-to-V, V-to-minor, V-to-major) organizing all Baker chord connections.

engine_rules.name: Classify every chord connection as one of three dominant-leading categories: dom-to-dom, dom-to-min, dom-to-maj
engine_rules.falsifier: A chord connection is analyzed outside these three categories
engine_rules.anchor: First we have dominant to dominant connections, second, we have dominant to minor connections and third, dominant to major connections. With these few chord connections you can build progressions around any song.

paragraphs.summary: Names the three-category chord-connection taxonomy.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: First we have dominant to dominant connections, second, we have dominant to minor connections and third, dominant to major connections.

chapter.title: Applying Chords, Introductions and Endings (Lessons 17-18)
chapter.summary: Applies the dominant-as-leading-chord and three-category taxonomy to real tunes via standard chord books; mandates transposition of intros and endings to six keys; establishes the ear-development loop of listening, chord-working, and humming against the chord.

sections.title: Applying chords to songs
sections.summary: Sets the practical application loop: take learned voicings immediately into real repertoire via substitution.

engine_rules.name: Apply learned voicings and substitutions to real tunes from sheet music immediately after drilling
engine_rules.falsifier: A chord substitution pattern is drilled in exercises only without being applied to a real song
engine_rules.anchor: Get four or five popular tunes ( sheet music ) or any kind of song that you like. Study the chord connections, then take your new chords and apply them to these songs.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes the real-repertoire application loop.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Get four or five popular tunes ( sheet music ) or any kind of song that you like. Study the chord connections, then take your new chords and apply them to these songs.

sections.title: Transpose intros and endings
sections.summary: Extends the all-keys transposition mandate explicitly to intro and ending phrases across six keys.

engine_rules.name: Transpose every intro and ending phrase to Db, Eb, F, G, Ab, Bb in addition to the home key

sections.title: Ear development by progression-building
sections.summary: States the ear-training rationale: harmonic vocabulary plus repeated listening-and-fitting is the loop that turns the chord catalog into musical intuition.

engine_rules.name: Develop harmonic ear by constantly listening to songs and working out chord progressions for them
engine_rules.anchor: A lot can be done toward developing your ear by constantly listening to songs and working out progressions for them.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes the ear-development loop of listening plus progression-working.

chapter.title: Chords with Two Names, Intros, Bop Blues, Endings and Sequences (Lessons 19-23)
chapter.summary: Installs the two-names principle (Gma6 = Emi7), root-omitted tritone-equivalent voicings (G7#5 = Db9b5), the bop blues reharmonization template, and eleven canonical sequence cycles. Marks the pivot away from diagram-dependence toward numbered-position recall.

sections.title: Chords with two names
sections.summary: Introduces the relative-substitution principle: one shape carries two functional identities depending on context.

engine_rules.name: Treat any maj6 voicing as interchangeable with its relative min7 a minor third below
engine_rules.falsifier: A maj6 shape is treated as having only one harmonic identity in a Baker substitution context
engine_rules.anchor: When we are in one key a chord may be Gma? while still in another key — the same chord has a different name, Emi7. Below I have analyzed the harmonic structure of these chords. You are to learn both names of these chords in all keys.

paragraphs.summary: Introduces the two-names relative-substitution principle.

sections.summary: Frames eleven canonical chord cycles as the harmonic skeletons of the standard repertoire.

chapter.title: Part Two Opens: Time Values, Wrist Development and Scales (Lessons 24-26)
chapter.summary: Pivots to single-note technique: mandates alternate picking as the universal right-hand rule, defines the 28-exercise mechanical foundation as the lifelong technical substrate, prescribes relaxed-slow-before-fast as the tempo-development principle, and names the symbol legend (X=open string, S=string, F=fingering).

sections.title: Up-and-down stroke mandate
sections.summary: Imposes alternate picking as the universal right-hand requirement for the entire rest of the book.

engine_rules.name: Apply alternate (up-and-down) picking to every exercise and solo in the book without exception
engine_rules.falsifier: A solo or exercise run is prescribed with single-direction picking rather than alternate strokes
engine_rules.anchor: Every exercise and solo in this book is to be played with an up and down stroke. In order to play with an up and down stroke you must start right now. Anything that you play from now on, you are to use up and down strokes.

paragraphs.summary: Mandates alternate picking for all exercises and solos.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Every exercise and solo in this book is to be played with an up and down stroke.

sections.title: Slow practice rule
sections.summary: Establishes the relaxed-slow-before-fast principle governing all exercise practice in Part Two.
key_phrases: can't play slowly can't play fast

engine_rules.name: Practice every exercise at the slowest relaxed tempo first; increase speed only when fully relaxed at slow tempo
engine_rules.falsifier: Baker prescribes beginning an exercise at a fast tempo before achieving relaxed slow-tempo execution
engine_rules.anchor: Take each exercise and practice it as slowly as possible. Only increase the tempo when you can play it relaxed at a slow tempo. Remember, if you cannot play an exercise slowly, you surely can't play it fast.

paragraphs.summary: States the slow-before-fast practice principle.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Take each exercise and practice it as slowly as possible. Only increase the tempo when you can play it relaxed at a slow tempo.

sections.title: Ear development practice
sections.summary: Codifies Baker's ear-training routine: records, horn solos, transcription, hum-then-play.

engine_rules.name: Develop ear by playing with records, stealing horn solos, and humming ideas against the chord before playing them
engine_rules.anchor: Practice playing your guitar with records, listen to solos by horn players, learn to steal solos from records. Anything that you hear another musician play, try to play it yourself. Strum the chords to any song that you like and hum ideas, — then apply the ideas to the guitar.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes the records-transcription-hum ear-training loop.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Practice playing your guitar with records, listen to solos by horn players, learn to steal solos from records.

chapter.title: Scale Runs, Minor/Dominant/Diminished Runs and Blues Pattern (Lessons 27-31)
chapter.summary: Drills scale, minor, dominant, and diminished runs with invariant fingering transposed by position-shift; narrows the blues transposition mandate to five horn-friendly keys; confirms that blues solos are built verbatim from the Lessons 27-30 run exercises.

sections.title: Chromatic fingering invariance
sections.summary: States the load-bearing position-system rule: one fingering shape transposed by position-shift covers all keys.

engine_rules.name: Use a single invariant fingering for each run type, transposing by position-shift rather than altering the shape
engine_rules.falsifier: Different fingering shapes are prescribed for the same run type in different keys
engine_rules.anchor: *You are to use the same fingering, up and down the fingerboard.

paragraphs.summary: States the invariant-fingering transposition rule.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: *You are to use the same fingering, up and down the fingerboard.

sections.title: Five blues keys
sections.summary: Narrows the blues transposition mandate to the five horn-friendly keys: F, G, Ab, Bb, C.

engine_rules.name: Restrict blues run and solo transposition to the five horn-friendly keys: F, G, Ab, Bb, C
engine_rules.falsifier: Blues solos are expected to be transposed to all twelve keys rather than the contracted five
engine_rules.anchor: The keys that the blues are played in mostly, are: —F, G, A', BS and C. So these are the keys that you are to concentrate on for now. These simple patterns that I have written out in the next few lessons are to be transposed to all five of these keys.

paragraphs.summary: Specifies the five horn-friendly blues keys as the target transposition set.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: The keys that the blues are played in mostly, are: —F, G, A', BS and C.

sections.title: Reuse of exercise runs
sections.summary: Confirms that blues solos are built from the exact runs of Lessons 27-30 with no modification.
key_phrases: runs just as they were in the exercise

engine_rules.name: Build blues solos using exercise runs verbatim from Lessons 27-30, selecting the appropriate run for each chord
engine_rules.falsifier: Blues solos are constructed from new melodic material outside the Lessons 27-30 run vocabulary
engine_rules.anchor: Now I am using these runs just as they were in the exercise, so all you have to do is to find the right one.

paragraphs.summary: Confirms exercise runs are used verbatim as blues solo material.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Now I am using these runs just as they were in the exercise, so all you have to do is to find the right one.

chapter.title: Review, Major/Minor/Dominant Runs, Run Connections and Blues Solos (Lessons 32-37)
chapter.summary: Extends the chords-with-two-names principle from chord work into solo lines via the relative-run substitution; codifies the always-alter-the-V rule and the Ami7→Cmi7→Gmaj run recipe; prescribes the strum-and-hum internalization drill; sets the one-day-per-key transposition schedule for six keys; and frames the fill-in blank-bar format for scaffolded improvisation.

sections.title: Relative run substitution
sections.summary: Extends the two-names principle into the solo domain: a min7 run substitutes freely for its relative major chord.
key_phrases: rule that applies to chords applies to runs

engine_rules.name: Substitute a min7 run for any major chord using the same relative rule as chords (Emi7 run over G major)
engine_rules.falsifier: A major chord passage requires a diatonic major run and prohibits the relative min7 run substitution
engine_rules.anchor: In Blues No. I for the first four bars I'm using an Emi7 run. You know that the chord for these four bars is G major for three and G7 for one. But Emi7 and Gma6 are the same (relatives), so it can be used as a major run (See Lesson 19). The same rule that applies to chords applies to runs.

engine_rules.name: Use Ami7 run over D7 and Gmi7 run over C7 as the blues bars 9-10 ii-for-V substitution
engine_rules.falsifier: The standard V7 and IV7 runs are used at blues bars 9-10 without the corresponding min7 substitution
engine_rules.anchor: In Blues progression sometimes at the ninth and tenth bar we use the V7 for one bar (which is D7 in the key of G major), and the IV7 for one bar (which is C7 in the key of G major), this allows you to use an Ami7 run for one bar and a Gmi7 run for one bar.

paragraphs.summary: States the relative-run substitution as the central improvisational license.
key_phrases: same rule chords applies to runs
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: The same rule that applies to chords applies to runs.

sections.title: Altered dominant principle
sections.summary: States the always-alter-the-V-into-I rule: dominant approaching major is always altered.

engine_rules.name: Always alter the dominant chord when it resolves to a major chord (G7#5+9 or G13b5+9 to Cma)
engine_rules.falsifier: An unaltered plain dom7 is prescribed at the V-to-I cadence point in a Baker arrangement
engine_rules.anchor: Notice that when connecting a dominant chord to a major the dominant in most of the time altered, (G7#529 to Cma ot G135¢9 to Cma). By altering chords like this they blend together perfectly. This same thing applies to solo work.

paragraphs.summary: States the always-alter-the-V-to-I rule.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Notice that when connecting a dominant chord to a major the dominant in most of the time altered, (G7#529 to Cma ot G135¢9 to Cma).

sections.title: Substituting minor-7 runs over V
sections.summary: Gives the concrete Ami7→Cmi7→G major run recipe over V→I.

engine_rules.name: Over V-to-I (D7→G major) use the Ami7→Cmi7→G major run sequence as the workhorse template
engine_rules.falsifier: A plain D-major or D-dominant run is used over D7 resolving to G without the Ami7/Cmi7 substitution
engine_rules.anchor: Whenever you have one or two bars of D7 going into G major, you may use an Ami7 run to a Cmi7 run which will blend right into a G major run.

paragraphs.summary: Gives the Ami7→Cmi7→Gmaj recipe for runs over V→I.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Whenever you have one or two bars of D7 going into G major, you may use an Ami7 run to a Cmi7 run which will blend right into a G major run.

sections.title: Hum runs against chords
sections.summary: Prescribes the strum-and-hum internalization drill for verifying run-against-chord sound.

engine_rules.name: Internalize run-against-chord sound by strumming chords and humming the run simultaneously until the run is heard before it is played
engine_rules.anchor: After you've learned the connections by heart, practice strumming the chords and humming the runs to yourself. By doing this, you can hear just how these runs sound against the chord progressions.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes the strum-and-hum internalization drill.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: practice strumming the chords and humming the runs to yourself. By doing this, you can hear just how these runs sound against the chord progressions.

sections.title: Fill-in solo method
sections.summary: Describes the scaffolded-improvisation format: blank bars carry a labeled run-type so the student generates phrases matching a specified run category.

engine_rules.name: Scaffold improvisation by filling labeled-blank bars with runs of the specified type from the exercise vocabulary
engine_rules.falsifier: Fill-in bars are completed with runs from outside the labeled run-type category
engine_rules.anchor: If you will notice I've written two or three bars, and in some places the bars are blank. This of course is where you fill in. Over these blank bars I have written the type of run I'd like you to use, so all you have to do is fill them in.

paragraphs.summary: Describes the blank-bar fill-in improvisation scaffold.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Over these blank bars I have written the type of run I'd like you to use, so all you have to do is fill them in.

sections.title: Blend over throw-together
sections.summary: States the overarching phrasing aesthetic: connection and blending of runs, not concatenation.

engine_rules.name: Join runs into connected melodic lines; reject concatenated runs that do not blend
engine_rules.falsifier: Runs are concatenated without connecting material and the result is presented as a satisfactory Baker solo
engine_rules.anchor: Above all, don't just throw the runs together. Make sure that they blend together as well as those that I have written.

paragraphs.summary: States the blending aesthetic for run connection.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Above all, don't just throw the runs together. Make sure that they blend together as well as those that I have written.

chapter.title: Riffs, Back to Vamp, Bridge Solo and Rhythm Changes (Lessons 38-43)
chapter.summary: Introduces the riff as 'ideas put together and forced against the chord'; establishes the two-position-per-key vocabulary for solo work (first-finger-behind-fret naming convention); defines C major as the lone single-position exception; installs the minor-for-dominant substitution in riff work; prescribes internalizing riffs by singing against the chord; and defines rhythm changes as vamps in Bb major.

sections.title: Definition of riff runs
sections.summary: Defines riff runs as non-diatonic ideas forced against the chord; contrasts with chord-derived runs.
key_phrases: don't have to be true to chord

engine_rules.name: License riff runs to contain non-diatonic tones; judge by fit against the chord rather than scale membership
engine_rules.falsifier: A riff is rejected because it contains tones outside the prevailing scale or chord
engine_rules.anchor: Riff Runs are only ideas put together and forced against the chord. They don't have to be true to the chord.

paragraphs.summary: Defines riff runs and licenses non-diatonic content.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Riff Runs are only ideas put together and forced against the chord. They don't have to be true to the chord.

sections.title: Why riffs replace chord runs in vamps
sections.summary: Explains the structural reason riffs dominate vamp solos: changes move too fast for chord-tone runs.

engine_rules.name: Use riffs rather than chord-derived runs as the primary melodic unit when vamp changes move faster than chord-tone runs allow
engine_rules.falsifier: Chord-tone runs are prescribed as the primary melodic unit over fast-moving vamp changes
engine_rules.anchor: The chord changes in Vamps move a little too fast for us to use chord runs, so we have to run ideas, which is where riffs come in,

paragraphs.summary: Explains why riffs replace chord runs in vamp contexts.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: The chord changes in Vamps move a little too fast for us to use chord runs, so we have to run ideas, which is where riffs come in,

sections.title: Defining position by first finger
sections.summary: Defines Baker's position-numbering convention: position is named by the fret behind which the first finger falls.

engine_rules.name: Name any playing position by the fret number behind which the first finger falls
engine_rules.anchor: The first six are in what is known as the 3rd position, because your first finger falls behind the 3rd fret on your Guitar. The 2nd six are in the 7th position, because your first finger falls behind the 7th fret on your Guitar. In other words, the fret that your first finger falls behind is the position that you are in.

paragraphs.summary: Defines the position-naming convention by first-finger fret placement.
key_phrases: first finger falls behind the fret
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: In other words, the fret that your first finger falls behind is the position that you are in.

sections.title: Two key positions per key
sections.summary: Establishes the two-position framework that organizes solo work in every key.

engine_rules.name: In any given key use the two governing positions for solo work: e.g., 3rd+7th in G, 4th+8th in Ab
engine_rules.falsifier: More than two governing positions are prescribed for solo work in a single key
engine_rules.anchor: In the key of G major, the 3rd and 7th positions are the most important in that key. In the key of Ab major it would be the 4th and 8th positions, in Bé major the 6th and 10th positions and so on.

paragraphs.summary: States two governing positions per key for all solo work.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: In the key of G major, the 3rd and 7th positions are the most important in that key.

sections.title: C major position exception
sections.summary: Flags C major as the lone single-position exception to the two-position rule: only 8th position is usable.

engine_rules.name: In C major use only the 8th position for riff solo work; the 12th position is out of practical range
engine_rules.falsifier: Two positions are prescribed for riff solos in C major including the 12th position
engine_rules.anchor: Now, when we get to the key of C major, we can use the 8th position, but we can't use the 12th position, because it is too far up on the fingerboard. So, this means that in the key of C major we only have one position for riff runs which is the 8th position.

paragraphs.summary: Carves out C major as the lone single-position exception.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: in the key of C major we only have one position for riff runs which is the 8th position.

sections.title: Internalize riffs by singing
sections.summary: Prescribes Baker's signature riff-internalization method: sing the riff against the chord until memorized.

engine_rules.name: Internalize every riff by singing it against the chord progressions until it can be sung and played simultaneously
engine_rules.anchor: Learn them all by heart, keep practicing them until you can sing them as you play them. Once you can sing them to yourself, try playing the chord progressions and singing the riffs together.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes the sing-against-chord internalization method for riffs.
key_phrases: chord progressions and singing riffs together
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: keep practicing them until you can sing them as you play them. Once you can sing them to yourself, try playing the chord progressions and singing the riffs together.

sections.title: Rhythm changes definition
sections.summary: Defines rhythm changes as vamp-style progressions conventionally played in Bb major.

engine_rules.name: Treat rhythm changes as vamp-style progressions and default their key to Bb major (concert)
engine_rules.falsifier: Rhythm changes are prescribed in a key other than Bb without explanation
engine_rules.anchor: Rhythm changes are pretty much the same as Vamps. The only difference is this, when a musician says' let's play some rhythm changes' they are always in B major (concert)

paragraphs.summary: Defines rhythm changes and pins their conventional key.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Rhythm changes are pretty much the same as Vamps. The only difference is this, when a musician says' let's play some rhythm changes' they are always in B major (concert)

chapter.title: Reviews, Solo Sketches, Riffs and Groove Riffs (Lessons 44-48)
chapter.summary: Introduces the additional 3rd-position (frets 3-6) scoped to Ab/Bb/C/Db/Eb; defines the groove riff as a first-and-last-course-matching riff repeated consecutively; requires groove-riff solos to be executed entirely in 3rd position; and reinforces the sing-riffs-over-progressions verification drill.
key_phrases: Ab Bb C Db Eb scope

sections.title: New 3rd position for solos
sections.summary: Introduces an additional position (3rd-6th frets) with explicit key-applicability constraints.

engine_rules.name: Apply the additional 3rd-fret position (frets 3-6) to Ab, Bb, C, Db, and Eb major; treat F and G as marginal
engine_rules.falsifier: The additional 3rd-fret position is prescribed as equally valid in all twelve keys including G and F
engine_rules.anchor: I am introducing a new position for solo work. This position is to be used for the keys of A4, Bé, C, Dé, and Ee major ( it can be used for F, and G major but it is a little out of range).

paragraphs.summary: Introduces and scopes the additional 3rd-fret position.
key_phrases: out of range for F and G
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: I am introducing a new position for solo work. This position is to be used for the keys of A4, Bé, C, Dé, and Ee major ( it can be used for F, and G major but it is a little out of range).

sections.title: Groove riff definition
sections.summary: Defines the groove riff: a riff whose first and last courses match, repeated consecutively.
key_phrases: first and last courses the same

engine_rules.name: Construct a groove riff so its first and last courses are identical, then repeat it consecutively across song boundaries
engine_rules.falsifier: A groove riff's first and last courses differ
engine_rules.anchor: When you go through this solo that I have written out, you will find that the first and the last courses are the same. This is known as a groove riff. Groove riffs are repeated consecutively.

paragraphs.summary: Defines the groove riff and its course-symmetry structure.
key_phrases: first and last courses the same
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: When you go through this solo that I have written out, you will find that the first and the last courses are the same. This is known as a groove riff. Groove riffs are repeated consecutively.

sections.title: Where to use groove riffs
sections.summary: Scopes groove riffs to blues and vamp forms, placed at song start and end.

engine_rules.name: Place groove riffs at the opening and closing of blues or vamp tunes only; do not use in other song forms
engine_rules.falsifier: Groove riffs are prescribed for ballad or standard-song-form choruses rather than blues/vamp forms
engine_rules.anchor: You usually start and end a song with groove riffs. These kind of riffs are only used against Blues and vamp changes (progression).

paragraphs.summary: Scopes groove riff placement to opening and closing of blues and vamp forms.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: You usually start and end a song with groove riffs. These kind of riffs are only used against Blues and vamp changes (progression).

sections.title: Solo entirely in 3rd position
sections.summary: Requires groove-riff solos to be executed entirely within the 3rd position (frets 3-6) without position shifting.

engine_rules.name: Execute groove-riff solos entirely within 3rd position (frets 3-6); do not leave this position for any part of the solo
engine_rules.falsifier: A groove-riff solo moves outside the 3rd position (frets 3-6) during any part of its execution
engine_rules.anchor: Now the tricky part about this solo is that it's all done in the 3rd position on your Guitar (between the 3rd and 6th fret )

paragraphs.summary: Locks groove-riff solos entirely within 3rd position.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Now the tricky part about this solo is that it's all done in the 3rd position on your Guitar (between the 3rd and 6th fret )

sections.title: Sing riffs over progressions
sections.summary: Specifies the ear-training verification drill for any forced-riff usage: sing riff against chord changes.
key_phrases: hear how riffs sound against chords

engine_rules.name: Verify every forced-riff usage by singing the riff against the chord progressions to confirm the combination sounds correct
engine_rules.anchor: study the riffs in each solo, then the chord progressions for those measures. Then sing the riffs while you play the chord progressions. This way you can hear just how the riffs sound against the chords.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes singing riffs against progressions as verification.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Then sing the riffs while you play the chord progressions. This way you can hear just how the riffs sound against the chords.

chapter.title: Building Around the Melody and Solo Patterns (Lessons 49-52)
chapter.summary: Closes the method with two solo-construction techniques: the implied-melody method (run chords around the melody under a 7th-11th-fret position lock so the listener still hears the tune) and the solo pattern (a per-course rhythmic frame held constant, with the first measure setting the timing for everything that follows). Also prescribes the singing procedure for inventing groove riffs.

sections.title: Implied-melody principle
sections.summary: Names the aesthetic goal of melody-building solos: the listener should still hear the tune even when it is not literally present.
key_phrases: hear the melody though it's not there

engine_rules.name: Build solos so the implied melody is audible to the listener even when the tune is not literally played
engine_rules.falsifier: A Baker melody-building solo departs from the tune so completely that the melody is no longer audible
engine_rules.anchor: Notice how you can always hear the melody though it's not really there.

paragraphs.summary: States the implied-melody aesthetic goal.
key_phrases: hear the melody though it's not really there
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Notice how you can always hear the melody though it's not really there.

sections.title: Build by running chords around melody
sections.summary: States Baker's method for constructing melody-based solos: run chords around the melody.

engine_rules.name: Construct melody-based solos by weaving chord runs around the stated melody, not by abandoning it
engine_rules.falsifier: A melody-based solo is constructed by replacing the melody with arbitrary runs rather than wrapping runs around it
engine_rules.anchor: I want you to make up a solo with this song, and build around the melody as I have done. All you have to do is run chords around it. Keep playing the melody and trying to fit in chord runs until you get some ideas,

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes running chords around the melody as the solo-construction method.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: All you have to do is run chords around it. Keep playing the melody and trying to fit in chord runs until you get some ideas,

sections.title: Position locked at 7th fret
sections.summary: Imposes a strict 7th-position (7th-11th fret) lock for melody-based solo work.

engine_rules.name: Execute melody-chord solos entirely between the 7th and 11th frets (7th position); do not leave this position
engine_rules.falsifier: A melody-chord solo moves below the 7th fret or above the 11th fret during its execution
engine_rules.anchor: Every note in this solo is between the 7th and 11th fret on your Guitar (the 7th position). You are not to leave this position to play any part of this solo,

paragraphs.summary: Locks melody-chord solos to the 7th-11th fret zone.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Every note in this solo is between the 7th and 11th fret on your Guitar (the 7th position). You are not to leave this position to play any part of this solo,

sections.title: Solo pattern definition
sections.summary: Defines a solo pattern as a per-course rhythmic frame held constant, with the first measure setting the timing.

engine_rules.name: Establish a solo pattern by using the first measure's rhythm as the constant frame for all subsequent measures in the course
engine_rules.falsifier: A solo pattern's rhythmic frame changes between measures within the same course
engine_rules.anchor: Notice how the first measure sets the pattern for all of the measures to follow. This is what we call solo patterns.

paragraphs.summary: States the first-measure-sets-the-pattern rule for solo patterns.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Notice how the first measure sets the pattern for all of the measures to follow. This is what we call solo patterns.

sections.title: Same timing, different notes
sections.summary: Operationalizes the solo-pattern rule: same rhythmic template, different melodic content bar to bar.

engine_rules.name: Within a solo pattern hold the rhythmic template constant across all bars while varying only the run content
engine_rules.falsifier: The rhythmic template changes between bars within a single solo pattern course
engine_rules.anchor: Take Example No. 1; in the first bar of the solo we have one quarter note, four sixteenth notes and three quarter triplets (lazy triplets). In the second bar you have the same identical timing, only the run is different.

paragraphs.summary: Operationalizes the solo pattern rule with a specific rhythmic example.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: In the second bar you have the same identical timing, only the run is different.

sections.title: Finding groove riffs by singing
sections.summary: Gives a concrete procedure for inventing groove riffs that fit a 12-bar form by singing against chord progressions.

engine_rules.name: Invent groove riffs by singing any riff against the blues chord progression until one fits the 12-bar sequence three times
engine_rules.anchor: take your Guitar and play the chord progressions to the Blues, and start singing any of your riffs, and keep singing them until you can get one that fits in the 12 bar sequence three times, as well as the one in Lesson No. 48.

paragraphs.summary: Prescribes the singing procedure for groove riff invention.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: take your Guitar and play the chord progressions to the Blues, and start singing any of your riffs, and keep singing them until you can get one that fits in the 12 bar sequence three times

sections.title: Review to keep learning
sections.summary: States the meta-rule about review-driven discovery governing how the entire book is to be used.

engine_rules.name: Return to earlier lessons repeatedly; each review pass reveals new content not absorbed in the first pass
engine_rules.anchor: That's why I always tell you to go back over these lessons so much, because I know that every time you review a lesson, you will learn something new about it.

paragraphs.summary: States the review-driven discovery meta-rule.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: every time you review a lesson, you will learn something new about it.
